subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage: Parul, you asked how I came back from failing two courses, so here it is, and I, Mridul, will be honest. My first thought was "I'm just not smart enough." But I made myself ask why, five times. Why did I fail? I missed the internal exams. Why? I was not in class for the first six weeks. Why? My grandfather was in hospital and I was travelling home every weekend and coming back late. Why did I not fix it? I never told any professor. Why? I was scared of sounding like I was making excuses. When I laid it out, it was about missed classes and not asking for help, not about ability. That felt different. Fixable.

qa.q: For how many weeks was Mridul absent from class at the start?
qa.a: Mridul was not in class for the first six weeks.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling at first about the failure?
qa.a: Mridul felt ashamed and doubtful about ability, thinking 'I'm just not smart enough' before asking why.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Mridul use next term to avoid a repeat, and why?
qa.a: Mridul could tell a professor or advisor early when something at home disrupts classes, because the chain shows that silence turned a short absence into a failed course.

qa.q: How might Parul see Mridul's story?
qa.a: Parul asked how Mridul came back and hears a plain account without excuses, so Parul may find it easier to trust that the failure was fixable.

grounding: Shows repeated why-questions leading from a failed result to missed early classes and reluctance to seek help, rather than to lack of ability.

subtype: Approach: talking honestly with an academic advisor [Action]
passage: Rehana, you asked what the first step was, and honestly it was the meeting with the advisor. I had avoided it for a week. Then on Wednesday I took my marksheet, printed, folded in a file, and knocked. I said, "I failed two subjects because I missed weeks after a family illness. I want to know what to do now." The advisor listened, did not sigh, and pulled up my record. They told me the dates for the backlog exams, how the credit counts work, and that I could take fewer courses next term. I wrote it all down. I walked out with a page of dates and a twenty-minute appointment for the following month. It felt smaller than I had feared. — Kavitha

qa.q: On which day did Kavitha meet the advisor?
qa.a: Kavitha went on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling before knocking on the advisor's door?
qa.a: Kavitha was nervous and reluctant, having avoided the meeting for a week and carrying the marksheet in a folded file.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kavitha add after the meeting, and why?
qa.a: Kavitha could form a small study group for the backlog subjects, because the advisor sorted the rules and dates but a group helps with the actual studying.

qa.q: How might the advisor have seen Kavitha's visit?
qa.a: The advisor listened, did not sigh and pulled up the record, so the advisor met a student with a clear question and gave practical details.

grounding: Shows a student going to an academic advisor with the marksheet, explaining honestly, and learning the practical options for backlogs and a lighter term.

subtype: Approach: avoidance and hiding the result [Pitfall]
passage:
Subject: Sorry I did not tell you

Dear Hansa,

You asked why I stopped picking up your calls. I failed one paper in November. I was so scared of Papa's face that I said nothing, and I told myself I would fix it quietly. The backlog form was due on 10 January, and I did not fill it. I thought, one more day. The deadline passed. Now the department says I will need to wait a whole extra term. Papa found out from the notice sent home, and he was not angry about the failure. He was hurt that I had hidden it. The silence cost more than the paper ever did. I am going to the advisor on Monday. Can you come with me?

Vasudha

qa.q: When was the backlog form due?
qa.a: The backlog form was due on 10 January.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when hiding the result?
qa.a: Vasudha felt afraid of Papa's reaction and hoped the problem could be fixed quietly.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vasudha have used in November, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could have told Papa or a trusted adult at once and asked the advisor about the form, because the deadline was the real danger and it needed people who could help.

qa.q: How does Papa see what happened?
qa.a: Papa was not angry about the failure but hurt that it was hidden, so Papa's worry is about the silence and not only the paper.

grounding: Shows hiding a failed result out of fear, skipping the forms, and finding that missed deadlines made things worse than the failure itself.

subtype: Approach: prioritising the courses needed first [Thinking]
passage: Advisor's note, written by Yogesh. Rajni came in after failing three courses and asked me to help her decide what to retake. Instead of choosing the easy ones, she asked for the course map. She sat with a highlighter and marked which of her failed courses unlock later ones and which do not. Two of the three lead into the fourth-semester subjects. The third is an elective. "Then these two first," she said. "The elective can wait, since nothing waits on it." I only confirmed the timetable for the backlog exam dates. She copied the dates into her phone, then asked whether a friend could share notes from the second course. I said yes and gave her the office number.

qa.q: How many failed courses lead into later subjects?
qa.a: Two of the three lead into the fourth-semester subjects.

qa.q: What is Rajni likely feeling as she marks the map?
qa.a: Rajni is likely determined and a little relieved, since sorting the courses gives a clear order out of a messy result.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rajni use if she still feels behind, and why?
qa.a: She could ask the advisor about a lighter course load, because clearing the blocking courses first may still need time and energy.

qa.q: How does Yogesh see Rajni's method?
qa.a: Yogesh watches a student who used the course map herself and only needed the dates confirmed, so Yogesh's role stays small.

grounding: Shows a student sorting failed courses by whether later courses depend on them, and retaking those first.

subtype: Approach: rebuilding routine with small checklists [Action]
passage: After the failed semester I made the list I now call my little list. Three lines only: go to every lecture, one hour of revision, five old questions. I wrote it on a sticky note and put it on my mirror. I had tried a big schedule before and it broke by the third day, so this time I kept it small on purpose. Some days I did only the first line and felt fine. My flatmate Shankar asked to look at it once, and I felt a little shy, but I showed him. By week three the ticks made a row, and I did not want to break it. On one awful day, when the lab report ate everything, I still got two of three. — Sangeeta

qa.q: What was written on Sangeeta's sticky note?
qa.a: The note said: go to every lecture, one hour of revision, five old questions.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Shankar asked to see the list?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt a little shy, but showed the list anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sangeeta add for the weeks ahead, and why?
qa.a: Sangeeta could add a weekly review of the ticks and adjust one line, because a small list keeps the habit alive but may need changes as courses get harder.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Sangeeta's list?
qa.a: Shankar asked to look at it once, which suggests curiosity and support, and saw that the list was small enough to keep.

grounding: Shows rebuilding a routine after a failed term with a very small daily checklist that stays possible even on a bad day.

subtype: Approach: overcorrecting with an extreme schedule [Pitfall]
passage: Imran taped a new chart above his desk in the Jaipur flat: 5 a.m. to 5 p.m., twelve hours of study, four backlogs and the fresh syllabus, all at once. "I'm going to make up the whole semester in a month," he told his flatmate Yogesh, who raised an eyebrow. "Twelve hours? You could not manage six last term." "Last term I was lazy." The first four days went well. On day nine he was reading the same paragraph three times. On day twelve he slept through the alarm, missed a class, and the chart stayed unticked all week. He pulled it off the wall, crumpled it, and dropped it in the bin. By Sunday he was not studying at all.

qa.q: How many hours of study did Imran's chart plan each day?
qa.a: The chart planned twelve hours of study.

qa.q: What is Imran feeling when he crumples the chart?
qa.a: Imran feels defeated and frustrated, tearing down the plan after failing to keep it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Imran use, and why?
qa.a: Imran could start with two hours a day and raise it slowly, because a plan that can be kept builds momentum where an extreme one collapses.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Imran's chart?
qa.a: Yogesh raises an eyebrow and points out that six hours was already too much last term, so Yogesh doubts the plan will hold.

grounding: Shows over-correcting after failure with an extreme timetable that collapses in the second week and is abandoned.

subtype: Approach: learning from past failure patterns [Thinking]
passage:
Chetan: I went through my last four semesters' marks last night
Pankaj: Scary? 
Chetan: A bit. But look. Sem 2 I was building the college fest website. Marks fell. Sem 4 I ran the part-time tutoring gig. Marks fell. Sem 3 nothing extra. Good marks
Pankaj: So it's not that you can't do it
Chetan: Right. It's every time a project lands on exam weeks
Pankaj: Are you going to quit the gig?
Chetan: No. I want to pause it for the two weeks around exams and tell my students in advance
Pankaj: That's smart. Put it in your calendar now
Chetan: Doing it. Also failing sem 5 was not random, apparently

qa.q: Which semester had nothing extra and good marks?
qa.a: Semester 3 had nothing extra and good marks.

qa.q: What is Chetan feeling about the pattern in the marks?
qa.a: Chetan feels relieved and a bit sobered, since the pattern shows the failure was not random and can be planned around.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chetan use besides pausing the gig, and why?
qa.a: Chetan could train a substitute for exam weeks or reduce hours earlier, because pausing suits a small gig but a bigger role may need cover.

qa.q: How might Chetan's tutoring students see the pause?
qa.a: Students told in advance can plan around a two-week break, which is kinder than a sudden disappearance during exam time.

grounding: Shows looking back over past terms and spotting that marks drop when a side project overlaps with exams, then planning to pause it.

subtype: Approach: seeking support from family and a counsellor [Action]
passage:
Lavanya: Told Mum last night. Finally
Hemant: How did it go?
Lavanya: She cried a bit, then asked what I needed. Not what I did wrong
Hemant: That's good
Lavanya: I said I feel ashamed. Every time I see my friends' results it hits again
Hemant: Did she say anything about that?
Lavanya: She said the campus counselling office is free and she'd like me to go. I booked for Thursday
Hemant: I'm proud of you
Lavanya: I'm nervous about it. I don't even know what to say
Hemant: You can start with what you told me
Lavanya: Yes. Then we make the plan for the backlog papers. Not alone this time

qa.q: Which day did Lavanya book the counselling visit?
qa.a: Lavanya booked the visit for Thursday.

qa.q: What is Lavanya feeling about going to counselling?
qa.a: Lavanya feels nervous and unsure what to say, though also relieved to have told Mum.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Lavanya add, and why?
qa.a: Lavanya could ask a trusted teacher to look at the backlog plan too, because a counsellor helps with stress and a teacher can check the study steps.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's mother have felt when she heard the news?
qa.a: Lavanya's mum cried a bit but then asked what Lavanya needed, which suggests worry mixed with care and no wish to blame.

grounding: Shows a student telling a parent about a failed term and using campus counselling so that the recovery plan is made with support.

subtype: Approach: reframing failure as a redirect [Thinking]
passage: Kalyani, you look down, so let old Jagdish tell you about my failed term. Second year, I took six courses and a hostel job. Two courses went badly. I sat on my bed for two days telling myself I was a failure. Then my warden, Mr Bhat, asked me a plain question: "If a friend brought you this marksheet, what would you say?" I said, "That six courses and a job was too much." He said, "So it's not a verdict. It's a message." I went and wrote it out: too heavy, and my way of studying did not suit that load. That was information I could act on. Blame gives you nothing to plan with. Information does.

qa.q: How many courses did Jagdish take in the second year?
qa.a: Jagdish took six courses.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling during the two days on the bed?
qa.a: Jagdish felt like a failure, sad and stuck, telling oneself the term proved something bad about oneself.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned the failure into a plan, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish answered the warden's question as if advising a friend, then wrote down that the load was too heavy, because that turned blame into information to act on.

qa.q: How might Mr Bhat have seen Jagdish's marksheet?
qa.a: Mr Bhat treated it as a message, not a verdict, asking a plain question and letting Jagdish reach the answer.

grounding: Shows treating a failed term as information about workload and study methods instead of a verdict, which makes planning possible without self-blame.

subtype: Approach: tracking weekly progress and adjusting [Revision]
passage: I sit next to Nilesh in the reading hall, so I noticed the sheet. Every Sunday he pulls out a page with two columns, one for targets and one for what actually happened: attendance, weekly test marks. I asked once, and he said it was so he doesn't fool himself. For three weeks his marks in thermodynamics stayed low while the other subjects moved up. Then on the third Sunday he crossed out "solo study" and wrote "group with Sabina and Tarun". By the next Sunday he was in the study room with two others, arguing over one derivation. I cannot say what he felt. I only saw the sheet change, and his tests improve. — Santosh

qa.q: Which subject stayed low for three weeks?
qa.a: Thermodynamics stayed low for three weeks.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt on the third Sunday, judging by what Santosh saw?
qa.a: Nilesh may have felt determined and a little frustrated, since he crossed out solo study and made a change, though Santosh admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nilesh try if the group also stalls, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh could ask the thermodynamics teacher for the weak topics, because a group shares confusion but a teacher can correct it.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Nilesh joining the group?
qa.a: Sabina gains a new member who argues over derivations from the first week, which could make the group livelier, though the passage does not show Sabina's view directly.

grounding: Shows weekly comparison of attendance and scores with targets, and swapping solo study for a group after repeated weak scores in one subject.
